exEn: Hi, Anna! Nice to see you.
note: Swedes say hej to everyone, from friends to the boss. It can also mean bye.

exEn: Bye, see you on Monday!
note: Also written hejdå.

exEn: A coffee, please.
note: Swedish has no everyday word for 'please': you add tack instead.

ex: – Är du svensk? – {Ja}, det är jag.
exEn: – Are you Swedish? – Yes, I am.
No, I don't drink coffee.
note: Before a noun, 'no' is ingen/inget/inga: inga pengar (no money).

exEn: Thank you so much for the present!
note: The t in mycket is silent.

exEn: Please, have a cookie!
note: Said when handing something over or inviting someone to go ahead. Also written var så god.

exEn: – Thanks for the help! – Don't mention it!
note: A reply to tack; literally 'no reason'.

exEn: Excuse me, is this seat free?
note: Used to get attention or to get past someone; to apologize, say förlåt.

exEn: Sorry I'm late!
note: From the verb förlåta (to forgive).

exEn: Okay, see you at seven.
note: Also written OK or ok.

exEn: Good morning! Did you sleep well?
note: Sounds like 'go-morron': the d and the g are usually silent.

exEn: Good evening! Have you booked a table?
note: Fairly formal; friends just say hej.

ex: Jag går och lägger mig nu. {God natt}!
exEn: I'm going to bed now. Good night!
note: Said when someone goes to bed. Also written godnatt.

exEn: Welcome to Sweden!
note: To more than one person, say välkomna!

exEn: How are you feeling today?
note: Asks how someone feels; Hur är det? is the more casual greeting.

exEn: I'm fine, thanks. And you?
My name is Anna. And you?
note: och is usually pronounced 'å'.

exEn: Hi! How are you doing?
note: A typical reply: Bra, tack! Och du?

exEn: Sorry, what's your name again?
note: vad is usually pronounced 'va': the d is silent.

exEn: Hi, my name is Ahmed.
note: jag is usually pronounced 'ja': the g is silent.

exEn: Hi, Sara! Nice to meet you!
note: A typical reply: Detsamma! (Likewise!)

ex: Du pratar bra svenska! {Var kommer du ifrån}?
exEn: You speak good Swedish! Where are you from?
note: A bit more formal: Varifrån kommer du?

ex: {Jag kommer från} Iran, men jag bor i Malmö.
exEn: I'm from Iran, but I live in Malmö.
See you tomorrow!
note: Literally 'we see each other': the -s makes the verb mutual.

exEn: Goodbye and take care!
note: det is pronounced 'de' in everyday speech.

exEn: – Would you like some coffee? – Yes, please!
No, thank you, I'm full.

ex: – Har du inte ätit? – {Jo}, det har jag.
exEn: – Haven't you eaten? – Yes, I have.
note: Use jo, not ja, to say yes to a question with inte (not) in it.

exEn: Hi there! What can I get you?
Thanks a million for a lovely evening!
note: Literally 'a thousand thanks'.

ex: {Tack för hjälpen}! Det var snällt av dig.
exEn: Thanks for the help! That was kind of you.
note: The h in hj is silent: hjälp sounds like 'yelp'.

exEn: Can you close the door, please?
note: Sounds pleading or insistent; in ordinary requests Swedes use tack or a polite question.

ex: – Vill du följa med på bio? – Ja, {gärna}!
exEn: – Do you want to come to the movies? – Yes, I'd love to!
note: Ja, gärna! = Yes, I'd love to! Irregular comparison: hellre (rather), helst (preferably).

exEn: I don't understand what you're saying.
note: inte (not) comes right after the verb.

exEn: Excuse me, can you speak more slowly?
note: långsammare = more slowly, from långsam (slow).

ex: Hej! {Talar du engelska}? Jag är turist.
exEn: Hi! Do you speak English? I'm a tourist.
note: In everyday speech: Pratar du engelska?

ex: {Jag pratar lite svenska}, men jag övar varje dag.
exEn: I speak a little Swedish, but I practice every day.
note: Names of languages are lowercase in Swedish: svenska, engelska.

ex: Förlåt, {vad sa du}? Jag hörde inte.
exEn: Sorry, what did you say? I didn't hear.
note: sa is the everyday form of sade (said).

ex: {Kan du hjälpa mig}? Jag hittar inte stationen.
exEn: Can you help me? I can't find the station.
note: mig is pronounced 'mej'.

exEn: I have to go now. Talk soon!
note: Literally 'we hear each other'; common at the end of calls and chats.

exEn: Thanks for today, and have a nice weekend!
note: Heard everywhere on Fridays: at work, in shops and in emails.

ex: – Bussen är försenad. – {Jaha}, då tar vi en taxi.
exEn: – The bus is late. – I see, then we'll take a taxi.

ex: {Tjena}, Erik! Ska vi ta en fika?
exEn: Hey, Erik! Shall we grab a coffee?
note: Casual, between friends. tj is a soft 'sh' sound.

exEn: I live in Gothenburg.
note: The g is usually silent: say “ja”.

exEn: Can you help me?
note: Pronounced “mej” (and sometimes spelled that way informally).

exEn: Anna, would you like some coffee?
note: Swedes say du to almost everyone, including teachers and bosses.

exEn: I miss you, Mom!
note: Pronounced “dej”.

exEn: He's my brother.
Do you know him?
note: Both o's are short å-sounds: “hånnåm”.

exEn: She speaks three languages.
I met her yesterday.

ex: Jag har en ny cykel. {Den} är blå.
exEn: I have a new bike. It's blue.
note: Use den for en-words (en bil → den) and det for ett-words (ett hus → det).

ex: Vi har köpt ett hus. {Det} är stort.
exEn: We've bought a house. It's big.
note: Usually pronounced “de”. Also a dummy subject: Det regnar (It's raining).

exEn: We eat dinner at six.
Do you want to come with us?
What are you guys doing this weekend?
note: For two or more people; ni as a polite “you” to one person sounds old-fashioned.

exEn: Kids, where are your shoes?
note: Possessive er/ert/era (er bil, ert hus, era skor); also the object form of ni: Jag ser er.

exEn: They're coming at seven.
note: de and dem are both pronounced “dom” in everyday speech.

exEn: We're meeting them on Saturday.
note: Pronounced “dom”, just like de.

exEn: You're not allowed to smoke here.
note: Means people in general, not the noun en man (a man).

exEn: She looks at herself in the mirror.
note: Pronounced “sej”. Used with reflexive verbs: han sätter sig, de känner sig trötta.

exEn: My sister lives in Norway.
note: mitt with ett-words, mina in the plural: min bil, mitt hus, mina barn.

exEn: Lisa, is this your jacket?
note: ditt with ett-words, dina in the plural: ditt namn, dina vänner.

exEn: His wife's name is Eva.
note: Never changes form: hans bil, hans hus, hans barn.

exEn: Her dad is from Chile.
note: henne = her as an object (Jag ser henne); hennes = her as a possessive (hennes bil).

exEn: Our apartment is pretty small.
note: vårt with ett-words, våra in the plural. Also the noun vår (spring).

exEn: Their house is near the lake.
He calls his mom every day.
note: Points back to the subject: Erik tar sin bil (his own), Erik tar hans bil (someone else's). Forms: sitt, sina.

exEn: I'll take this sweater.
note: The noun takes the definite form: den här bilen. Plural: de här bilarna.

exEn: This is my friend Sara.
note: With an ett-noun in the definite form: det här huset. Det här är … = This is …

exEn: What's that?
note: den där with en-words, de där in the plural: den där mannen (that man).

exEn: Is anyone home?
note: Often said “nån” in speech.

exEn: Would you like something to drink?
note: Often said “nåt” in speech; någonting means the same.

exEn: I have a few questions.
note: Plural; in questions it means “any”: Har du några syskon?

exEn: Nobody knows where he is.
note: inget with ett-words, inga in the plural: ingen tid, inget vatten, inga pengar.

exEn: I have nothing to do.
note: ingenting means the same and is very common in speech: Jag vet ingenting.

exEn: There are no buses at night.
Everyone is welcome!
note: With a singular noun use all (en-words) or allt (ett-words): all mat, allt vatten.

exEn: Thanks for everything!
I work out every day.
note: Never changes, and the noun stays indefinite: varje dag, varje år.

exEn: Can we meet another day?
note: annat with ett-words, andra in the plural and after den/det: ett annat hus, den andra bilen.

exEn: What do you want to eat?
note: Usually pronounced “va”.

exEn: Who is it?
Whose phone is this?
Where do you live?
note: var = where (at a place), vart = where (to): Var är du? Vart ska du?

exEn: Where are you going this summer?
note: Only for movement towards a place. Many Swedes say vart for var in speech, but keep them apart in writing.

exEn: Where are you from?
note: In speech often split up: Var kommer du ifrån?

exEn: When does the movie start?
How do I get to the station?
Why are you learning Swedish?
note: Answer with därför att … or eftersom … (because …).

exEn: Which bus should I take?
note: vilket with ett-words, vilka in the plural: Vilket hus? Vilka dagar?

exEn: How much water do you drink?
note: For things you can't count (vatten, tid, pengar); for things you can count use hur många.

exEn: How many siblings do you have?
How old are you?
note: gammal agrees with what you ask about: Hur gammalt är huset? Hur gamla är barnen?

exEn: It's zero degrees outside.
note: Phone numbers are read digit by digit: noll-sju-noll …

ex: Vi har {ett} barn och en hund.
exEn: We have one child and a dog.
note: Ett is the counting form. With en-words say en: en bil, ett hus.

exEn: Two coffees, please!

ex: Jag har bott i Sverige i {tre} år.
exEn: I've lived in Sweden for three years.
The bus leaves in four minutes.
note: As a noun it is en fyra: Jag tar fyran = I'll take the number 4 (bus or tram).

exEn: I have five cousins.
A table for six, please.
I wake up at seven every day.
note: sj is the special sj-sound ɧ, not an English sh.

exEn: See you around eight!
I work from nine to five.
note: In casual speech often “nie”.

exEn: I'll be there in ten minutes.
note: In casual speech often “tie”. En tia = a ten-kronor coin.

exEn: A soccer team has eleven players.
It's twelve o'clock.
I have thirteen new emails.

ex: Jag var {fjorton} när vi flyttade hit.
exEn: I was fourteen when we moved here.
note: Say “fjoo-ton”: the r melts into the t. Fjorton dagar = two weeks.

ex: Det tar {femton} minuter att gå dit.
exEn: It takes fifteen minutes to walk there.
She's sixteen years old.
I live at Storgatan 17.
note: The u is short here: “shutt-on”, unlike the long u in sju.

ex: I Sverige får man rösta när man är {arton}.
exEn: In Sweden you can vote when you're eighteen.
note: Spelled arton, with a long a: “aa-ton”.

exEn: There are nineteen students in the class.
It costs twenty kronor.
note: tj is the soft tj-sound ɕ. 21–29 are one word: tjugoett, tjugotvå …

exEn: We've been waiting for thirty minutes!
note: Usually said “tretti”: the final o is dropped.

exEn: I work forty hours a week.
note: Said “förti”.

exEn: The speed limit here is fifty.
note: Usually said “femti”.

exEn: An hour has sixty minutes.
note: Usually said “sexti”.

exEn: I have seventy kronor left.
note: Usually said “sjutti”, with a short u.

exEn: Grandma turns eighty on Saturday.
note: Usually said “åtti”.

exEn: He lived to be ninety.
note: Usually said “nitti”.

exEn: I've said it a hundred times!
note: Hundreds are one word: tvåhundra, femhundra.

exEn: A thousand people live in the village.
note: Thousands are one word: tvåtusen, femtusen.

exEn: He won a million on the lottery.
note: A noun: två miljoner. A billion is en miljard.

ex: Kan du {räkna} till tio på svenska?
exEn: Can you count to ten in Swedish?
note: räkna med = to count on, to expect.

exEn: Can I have your number?
note: nummer = a phone, house or size number; tal = a number in maths; siffra = a digit.

ex: Tänk på ett {tal} mellan ett och tio.
exEn: Think of a number between one and ten.
note: Also 'speech': hålla tal. På 1990-talet = in the 1990s.

exEn: The code has four digits.
note: A single written digit: 25 is a tal with two siffror.

ex: Är det {första} gången du är i Sverige?
exEn: Is this your first time in Sweden?
note: Dates use ordinals: den första maj = May 1st.

exEn: Take the second street on the left.
note: Also means 'other': de andra = the others.

exEn: My birthday is on April third.
note: Fractions add -del: en tredjedel (⅓), en fjärdedel (¼).

ex: Det här är min {fjärde} kopp kaffe idag.
exEn: This is my fourth cup of coffee today.
We live on the fifth floor.
Sweden's National Day is June sixth.
I'm in seventh heaven!
My son is in eighth grade.

ex: Det regnar för {nionde} dagen i rad.
exEn: It's raining for the ninth day in a row.
We're celebrating our tenth wedding anniversary.
The course starts on January eleventh.
December is the twelfth month of the year.
note: From 13th on, add -de: trettonde. 20th = tjugonde, 21st = tjugoförsta.

exEn: See you in half an hour.
note: Time trap: halv tre = 2:30 (half an hour before three).

ex: Vill du ha {hälften} av min smörgås?
exEn: Do you want half of my sandwich?
note: Mostly used as hälften: hälften av … = half of …

exEn: We're staying a couple of days.
note: Means 'a few', not exactly two. Also 'a pair': ett par skor.

exEn: My phone only has ten percent left.
note: The plural is the same: fem procent.

ex: Jag har varit i Stockholm två {gånger}.
exEn: I've been to Stockholm twice.
note: en gång = once, två gånger = twice. In maths: tre gånger fyra = 3 × 4.

ex: Jag dricker kaffe tre gånger om {dagen}.
exEn: I drink coffee three times a day.
note: Per day = om dagen (also i veckan, i månaden, om året). In speech the g is often silent: 'da'.

exEn: We're on vacation for four weeks.
note: Swedes often talk in week numbers: Vi ses vecka 32.

ex: Jag får lön en gång i {månaden}.
exEn: I get paid once a month.
My daughter is five years old.
note: Same form in the plural: ett år, två år. i år = this year.

exEn: What are you doing today?
note: Also written i dag.

exEn: I met Anna yesterday.
note: Also written i går. The day before yesterday = i förrgår.

exEn: See you tomorrow!
note: Also written i morgon. Sounds like 'imorron'. The day after tomorrow = i övermorgon.

exEn: I have to go now.
note: just nu = right now.

exEn: See you soon!

ex: Jag börjar på ett nytt jobb på {måndag}.
exEn: I'm starting a new job on Monday.
note: Days and months have no capital letter in Swedish. In speech the g is usually dropped: 'månda'.

exEn: We have Swedish class on Tuesdays.
note: på tisdag = this (coming) Tuesday; på tisdagar = on Tuesdays, every week.

exEn: Is it Wednesday already?
note: Jokingly called lillördag ('little Saturday').

exEn: Many people eat pea soup on Thursdays.
note: rs sounds like sh, and the g is usually dropped: 'toosh-da'.

exEn: Finally, it's Friday!
What are you doing on Saturday?
note: Many Swedish kids only get candy on Saturdays: lördagsgodis.

ex: På {söndag} äter vi middag hos mormor.
exEn: On Sunday we're having dinner at Grandma's.
note: i söndags = last Sunday; på söndag = this Sunday. Works for every day: i måndags, i fredags …

exEn: I never work on weekends.
note: Also a public holiday period: julhelgen = the Christmas holidays.

exEn: The bus runs every fifteen minutes on weekdays.
note: Also 'everyday life': i vardagen = in everyday life.

exEn: I shower every morning.
note: Pronounced 'morron'. i morgon = tomorrow, but i morse = this morning.

exEn: I only work in the mornings.
note: The part of the day before lunch, roughly 9 to 12. Early morning is morgon.

exEn: See you this afternoon!
note: i eftermiddag = this afternoon; på eftermiddagen = in the afternoon.

exEn: I work out in the evenings.
We're staying one night in Gothenburg.
note: Irregular plural with a vowel change: nätter.

exEn: I missed the bus this morning.
note: Only for a morning that has already passed.

exEn: What are you doing tonight?
note: Also written ikväll.

exEn: I slept badly last night.
note: The night that just passed or the coming night: context tells which.

exEn: What are you doing this weekend?
note: Also 'last weekend': Vad gjorde du i helgen?

exEn: The store closes at eight o'clock.
note: klockan åtta = at eight o'clock, with no preposition. Swedes use the 24-hour clock in writing: 20.00.

exEn: Excuse me, what time is it?
note: Also: Hur mycket är klockan? Answer: Klockan är tre (It's three o'clock).

exEn: The movie is two hours long.
note: en halvtimme = half an hour.

ex: Det tar fem {minuter} att gå dit.
exEn: It takes five minutes to walk there.
Wait a second!
note: 'Second' as in second place is andra.

exEn: It's a quarter past three.
note: kvart över tre = 3:15, kvart i fyra = 3:45.

exEn: The meeting starts at half past two.
note: Trap! Swedish counts half an hour towards the next hour: halv tre = 2:30, not 3:30.

exEn: What time does the movie start?
note: Very common in speech. Vilken tid …? and När …? also work.

exEn: We're taking an early train.
note: tidigt is also the adverb: Jag går upp tidigt (I get up early). tidigare = earlier.

exEn: Sorry I'm late!
note: It's late = Det är sent. Don't confuse it with sen = then (short for sedan).

ex: I {januari} är det mörkt och kallt.
exEn: In January it's dark and cold.
note: Months have no capital letter in Swedish: i januari = in January.

exEn: February is the shortest month of the year.
I moved to Sweden in March.
Easter is in April this year.
We're getting married in May.
School ends in June.
Many Swedes are on vacation in July.
In August we eat crayfish.
My birthday is on September 5th.
note: Dates: den femte september (written 5 september) = September 5th.

exEn: The leaves turn yellow in October.
It's so dark in November.
Lucia is celebrated on December 13th.
What's the date today?
note: Same form in the plural: två datum. Dates are often written year first: 2026-06-06.

exEn: Happy birthday!
note: In speech often 'fölsedag'.

exEn: It's Mom's birthday on Sunday.
note: När fyller du år? = When is your birthday? Hon fyller 30 = She's turning 30.

exEn: In spring the days get longer.
note: Same spelling as vår (our). i våras = last spring.

ex: Vi ska åka till Italien i {sommar}.
exEn: We're going to Italy this summer.
note: i sommar = this summer, i somras = last summer. Plural: somrar.

exEn: It rains a lot in the fall.
Winter is long in Sweden.
note: The e drops before an ending: vintern, vintrar.

exEn: I'm getting off at the next stop.
note: The noun has no definite ending: nästa vecka (next week). Compare förra veckan.

exEn: I was in Stockholm last week.
note: The noun takes the definite form: förra veckan, förra året (last week, last year).

ex: Hur {länge} har du bott i Sverige?
exEn: How long have you lived in Sweden?
note: Only about time; for length use lång. Ha det så länge! = Bye for now!

ex: Jag läste en {stund} innan jag somnade.
exEn: I read for a while before I fell asleep.

ex: Hela {familjen} äter middag ihop på söndagar.
exEn: The whole family has dinner together on Sundays.
note: Stress on the second syllable: fa-MILJ. The final j is pronounced.

exEn: I call Mom every evening.
note: Often used like a name, without min: Mamma är hemma. The formal word is mor.

ex: {Pappa}, kan du hämta mig efter skolan?
exEn: Dad, can you pick me up after school?
note: Often used like a name: Pappa lagar mat. The formal word is far.

exEn: My parents live in Gothenburg.
note: Mostly used in the plural: föräldrar (the e drops). Stress on -äl-.

exEn: Our son starts school this fall.
note: Plural with umlaut: söner. Many surnames end in -son: Andersson = Anders's son.

exEn: Their daughters are in the same class.
note: Plural with umlaut: döttrar, döttrarna.

ex: Min {bror} är två år äldre än jag.
exEn: My brother is two years older than me.
note: Irregular: brodern, bröder. storebror = big brother, lillebror = little brother.

ex: Jag har två {systrar} och en bror.
exEn: I have two sisters and a brother.
note: The e drops in the plural: systrar. storasyster = big sister, lillasyster = little sister.

exEn: Do you have any brothers or sisters?
note: Covers both brothers and sisters. Same form in the plural: två syskon.

exEn: How many children do you have?
note: Same form in the plural: ett barn, två barn. barnen = the children.

ex: {Mormor} bor i ett litet hus på landet.
exEn: Grandma lives in a small house in the country.
note: mor + mor: your mother's mother. Used like a name; the definite forms are rare.

exEn: Grandpa taught me to ride a bike.
note: mor + far: your mother's father. Swedish always shows which side of the family.

exEn: Grandma bakes the best cinnamon buns in the world.
note: far + mor: your father's mother.

exEn: My grandfather turns ninety this year.
note: far + far: your father's father.

ex: Jag och min {kusin} är lika gamla.
exEn: My cousin and I are the same age.
note: Stress on the second syllable: ku-SIN.

exEn: We're celebrating Christmas at Aunt Eva's.
note: mor + syster. Your father's sister is your faster.

exEn: My aunt has three dogs.
note: far + syster. Nothing to do with English "faster"!

ex: Jag bodde hos min {morbror} i ett år.
exEn: I lived with my uncle for a year.
note: mor + bror. Your father's brother is your farbror.

exEn: My uncle drives a taxi in Stockholm.
note: far + bror. Children also call any older man farbror.

ex: De har fyra barn och tio {barnbarn}.
exEn: They have four children and ten grandchildren.
note: barn + barn: a child's child. Same form in the plural.

exEn: All our relatives are coming to the wedding.
note: One relative is en släkting. vara släkt med = to be related to.

ex: Min {man} och jag har två barn.
exEn: My husband and I have two kids.
note: Irregular plural: män, männen. min man = my husband. Not the pronoun man (one, you).

exEn: Who is the woman in the picture?
note: In everyday speech, a young woman is often called tjej.

exEn: The boy plays soccer every Saturday.
note: In everyday speech, kille is more common, especially for teens and young men.

exEn: They had a baby girl in May.
note: A bit formal. In everyday speech, tjej is more common.

ex: Vem är {killen} som pratar med Sara?
exEn: Who's the guy talking to Sara?
note: Exception: the k is hard, not a tj-sound. Also boyfriend: Hon har en kille.

exEn: She's a really nice girl.
note: The everyday word for a girl or young woman. Also girlfriend: Han har en tjej.

exEn: The baby is finally asleep!
note: Also spelled bäbis.

exEn: We have two teenagers at home.
note: From tonår (the teens): the numbers thirteen to nineteen all end in -ton.

exEn: Two adults and one child, please.
note: Often used as a noun: en vuxen, två vuxna.

exEn: She's a wonderful person.
note: Plural människor = people. Exception: sk is a sj-sound here, "männisha".

exEn: The car has room for five people.
note: Stress on the second syllable: per-SON. rs is pronounced like sh.

ex: Det var mycket {folk} på stan idag.
exEn: There were lots of people in town today.
note: Used with mycket, not många: mycket folk. Also a people or nation: det svenska folket.

exEn: Can you spell your name?
note: förnamn = first name, efternamn = last name. To ask someone's name, say Vad heter du?

exEn: Where were you born?
note: Swedish uses the present tense: Jag är född 1995 = I was born in 1995.

exEn: She's my best friend.
note: Plural vänner. kompis is more casual.

ex: Jag ska träffa några {kompisar} i kväll.
exEn: I'm meeting some friends tonight.
note: The everyday word for friend, used at all ages.

exEn: Her boyfriend is from Finland.
note: Only a romantic partner; a male friend is en vän or en kompis. In speech, often min kille.

ex: Min {flickvän} och jag har flyttat ihop.
exEn: My girlfriend and I have moved in together.
note: Only a romantic partner; a female friend is en vän or en kompis. In speech, often min tjej.

exEn: Are you married or living together?
note: Short for sammanboende: an unmarried partner you live with. Very common in Sweden, also on official forms.

ex: Hon bor i Lund med sin {make}.
exEn: She lives in Lund with her husband.
note: Formal or written. In everyday speech, people say min man. makar = a married couple.

exEn: This is my wife, Lena.
note: hustru is a more formal word for wife. Before a surname, fru means Mrs.

ex: Du får gärna ta med din {partner}.
exEn: You're welcome to bring your partner.
note: A neutral word for a spouse, boyfriend or girlfriend. Plural partner or partners.

exEn: I don't know my neighbors.
note: bo granne med = to live next door to.

ex: Mina föräldrar har varit {gifta} i trettio år.
exEn: My parents have been married for thirty years.
note: The g is soft: "jift". gift med = married to. The opposite is ogift (unmarried).

ex: Hon är {skild} och har två barn.
exEn: She's divorced and has two kids.
note: From skilja sig (to get divorced). sk before i is a sj-sound.

ex: Jag har varit {singel} i två år.
exEn: I've been single for two years.
note: Usually without en: Är du singel? On official forms, the word is ogift (unmarried).

exEn: They got married last summer.
note: gifta sig med = to marry someone. The g is soft. Gift dig med mig! = Marry me!

ex: Vi är bjudna på {bröllop} i juni.
exEn: We're invited to a wedding in June.
note: Same form in the plural: två bröllop.

ex: Vi ska {hälsa på} mormor i helgen.
exEn: We're going to visit Grandma this weekend.
note: Stress on på. With på unstressed, hälsa på någon means to say hello to someone.

ex: Vem {tar hand om} barnen när ni jobbar?
exEn: Who takes care of the kids when you're working?
note: Irregular like ta: tog, tagit. Ta hand om dig! = Take care!

exEn: Welcome to our new home!
note: Going home is hem, being at home is hemma: Jag går hem. Jag är hemma.

ex: De bor i ett stort {hus} på landet.
exEn: They live in a big house in the country.
We rent an apartment downtown.
note: En tvåa is a two-room apartment, en trea a three-room one; the kitchen isn't counted.

exEn: The apartment has three rooms and a kitchen.
We have breakfast in the kitchen.
note: k before ö is soft: tj-sound.

exEn: The bathroom is on the left.
My bedroom is quite small.
We watch TV in the living room.
note: In everyday speech the g is usually dropped.

exEn: Leave your shoes in the hallway, please.
note: The entrance area of a home, where you take off your shoes and coat.

exEn: May I use the bathroom?
note: Informally called toa.

exEn: Close the door, there's a draft!

ex: Öppna {fönstret}, det är varmt här inne.
exEn: Open the window, it's warm in here.
note: Definite fönstret: the e drops before -et.

exEn: The children are sitting on the floor playing.
note: A floor of a building (a level) is en våning.

exEn: I live on the third floor.
note: The surface you walk on is golv.

exEn: The lamp hangs from the ceiling.
note: Tak means both roof and ceiling.

exEn: The picture is hanging on the wall.
note: vägg is the wall of a room or building; a free-standing stone wall is en mur.

ex: Hissen är trasig, så vi tar {trappan}.
exEn: The elevator is broken, so we're taking the stairs.
note: Jag bor två trappor upp = I live two floors above the ground floor.

exEn: I'm lying in bed reading.
The food is on the table.
Grab a chair and sit down!

ex: Vi sitter i {soffan} och tittar på film.
exEn: We're sitting on the sofa watching a movie.
note: Swedes usually sit i soffan (in the sofa).

exEn: Grandpa is sitting in the armchair reading.
note: From French fauteuil; stressed on the last syllable.

exEn: Turn on the lamp, it's dark in here.
note: Turn the light on/off: tända/släcka lampan.

exEn: The plates are in the cupboard on the left.
Hang your jacket in the closet.
note: Also the cloakroom at a restaurant or theater.

exEn: The books are on the shelf.
My sweaters are in the dresser.
note: Also means agency or office: resebyrå (travel agency).

exEn: She looks at herself in the mirror.
note: Plural speglar: the e drops.

exEn: The cat is lying on the rug.
Can you draw the curtains?
note: dra för / dra ifrån gardinerna = close / open the curtains.

exEn: He's in the shower right now.
note: The verb is duscha: Jag duschar på morgonen.

exEn: The kids are having a bath in the tub.
The soap is by the sink.
note: A kitchen sink is en vask or en diskho.

exEn: The faucet is dripping.
note: Also means a crane (for lifting).

exEn: I can't find my keys!
note: Plural nycklar: the e drops.

exEn: We're having coffee on the balcony.
note: Stressed on the last syllable.

exEn: Grandma has a lovely garden.
note: The d in träd is silent: trä-gård.

exEn: The car is in the garage.
note: Said the French way, ending in the sj-sound.

exEn: The bikes are in the basement.
note: k before ä is soft: tj-sound. Plural källare, källarna.

exEn: The Christmas things are up in the attic.
note: Looks and sounds like vind (wind). In the attic = på vinden.

exEn: I want a soft pillow.
The child sleeps under a thick duvet.
note: A thin blanket is en filt.

exEn: I change the sheets every week.
Bring a towel to the beach.
note: The two d's merge into one: han-duk.

exEn: Wash your hands with soap and water.
We're out of shampoo.
note: Stressed on the first syllable, unlike English.

exEn: Have you packed your toothbrush?
We need to buy toothpaste.

ex: Vi har köpt nya {möbler} till vardagsrummet.
exEn: We've bought new furniture for the living room.
note: English 'furniture' is usually möbler (plural).

exEn: The computer is on the desk.

ex: Vi tar {hissen} upp till femte våningen.
exEn: We're taking the elevator up to the fifth floor.
The washing machine is broken again.
We clean every Saturday.
note: Used for cleaning a room or home; washing something is tvätta.

exEn: I vacuumed the whole apartment yesterday.
note: Conjugated like suga: dammsög, dammsugit. Dammsugade is also used.

exEn: I have to do the laundry tonight.
note: On its own it often means to do the laundry. Washing the dishes is diska.

exEn: Don't forget to make your bed!
She's a teacher.
note: Irregular: är, var, varit. In speech, är often sounds like "e".

ex: Vi {har} en hund och två katter.
exEn: We have a dog and two cats.
note: Also the helper verb for the perfect: Jag har ätit (I have eaten).

exEn: What are you doing this weekend?
note: The g is soft: "jöra". Irregular: gjorde, gjort (gj sounds like j).

exEn: I walk to work every day.
note: Irregular: gick, gått. By car, bus or train, use åka. Jag måste gå = I have to leave.

exEn: When is the bus coming?
note: Irregular: kom, kommit. Kommer att + verb = will: Det kommer att regna.

exEn: I can't come tomorrow.
note: No att before the next verb: Jag kan simma. Jag kan svenska = I know Swedish.

exEn: I want to learn Swedish.
note: To want something is vilja ha: Jag vill ha te. Irregular: ville, velat.

exEn: I'm going to call Mom after work.
note: For plans (I'm going to …). Skulle also means "would". Also spelled skall; the infinitive skola is rare.

exEn: We have to buy groceries today.
note: Same form in present and past. "Don't have to" is behöver inte.

exEn: Do you need help?
note: Stress on the second syllable: be-HÖ-va. Du behöver inte = you don't have to.

exEn: I woke up at six this morning.
note: To wake someone else up is väcka.

ex: Jag {stiger upp} klockan sju varje dag.
exEn: I get up at seven every day.
note: Stress on upp. Irregular: steg, stigit. Gå upp means the same and is just as common.

exEn: I always shower in the morning.
We ate pizza last night.
note: Irregular: åt, ätit.

exEn: I drink coffee every morning.
note: Irregular: drack, druckit.

exEn: Did you sleep well last night?
note: Irregular: sov, sovit. Sov gott! = Sleep well!

exEn: She goes to bed early.
note: sig changes with the person: jag går och lägger mig, du … dig. Past also written lade.

exEn: Where do you live?
note: Where you live is bo; being alive is leva.

exEn: What's your dog's name?
note: Also for words: Vad heter "dog" på svenska?

exEn: My grandmother is still alive.
note: Being alive or living a life is leva; where you live is bo.

exEn: Did you see the movie yesterday?
note: Irregular: såg, sett. Se upp! = Watch out!

exEn: We watch TV every evening.
note: titta på = look at, watch. Titta! = Look!

exEn: Can you hear me?
note: Hearing just happens; listening on purpose is lyssna.

exEn: I listen to music on the bus.
note: Listen to = lyssna på: Lyssna på mig!

ex: Jag {läser} en bra bok just nu.
exEn: I'm reading a good book right now.
note: Also "to study" a subject: Hon läser medicin.

exEn: Can you write your name here?
note: Irregular: skrev, skrivit.

ex: Vi {pratade} i telefon i en timme.
exEn: We talked on the phone for an hour.
note: The everyday word; tala is more formal.

exEn: She speaks four languages.
note: More formal than prata. Tala om can also mean "to tell".

exEn: She says she's sick.
note: Usually pronounced "säja". Past: sa (more formal: sade).

exEn: Do you understand what I mean?
note: Inflected like stå: förstod, förstått. Stress on -stå.

exEn: I don't know where he lives.
note: Irregular: vet, visste, vetat. To know a person is känna.

exEn: Do you know Anna?
note: k before ä is soft: tj-sound. Jag känner mig trött = I feel tired.

exEn: I think the movie was good.
note: For opinions. To believe is tro; to think (use your mind) is tänka.

exEn: I like traveling.
note: Stress on om. Gilla means the same but is more casual.

exEn: Do you like sushi?
note: g before i is soft: "jilla".

exEn: I love you.
note: Also for things you really like: Jag älskar glass!

exEn: I take the bus to school.
note: Irregular: tog, tagit.

exEn: She gave me a book.
note: g before e is soft: "je". Irregular: gav, gett (also givit).

exEn: May I sit here?
note: Two meanings: may (Får jag …?) and to get (Jag fick ett brev). Irregular: fick, fått.

exEn: He's helping his mom in the garden.
note: The h is silent: "jälpa". Hjälp! = Help!

exEn: My sister works at a hospital.
note: In everyday speech, jobba is more common.

exEn: I work from home on Fridays.
note: The everyday word for arbeta.

exEn: I bought a new jacket yesterday.
note: k before ö is soft: tj-sound.

exEn: Have you paid the rent?
note: Stress on the second syllable: be-TA-la.

exEn: The coffee costs thirty kronor.
note: Hur mycket kostar det? = How much is it?

exEn: Can you open the window?
note: The adjective is öppen: Affären är öppen.

exEn: The store closes at six.
note: Stänga av = to turn off: Stäng av tv:n!

exEn: The movie starts at eight.
note: Often without att: Det började regna (It started to rain).

exEn: School finishes at three.
note: Sluta! = Stop it! Sluta röka = to quit smoking.

exEn: I can't find my keys!
note: Jag hittar inte = I can't find (no kan needed).

exEn: What are you looking for?
note: Usually leta efter = look for. When you succeed, you hitta (find) it.

exEn: How do you use this app?
note: Past: använde, supine: använt.

exEn: Dad is fixing the bike in the garage.
note: Laga mat = to cook. Otherwise laga means to fix or repair.

exEn: There's milk in the fridge.
note: Det finns = there is/are. Irregular: finns, fanns, funnits.

exEn: What happened?
note: Vad har hänt? = What has happened?

exEn: She's sitting on the sofa, reading.
note: Irregular: satt, suttit. To sit down is sätta sig.

ex: Vi {stod} i kö i tjugo minuter.
exEn: We stood in line for twenty minutes.
note: Irregular: stod, stått. Det står … = it says … (in a text).

exEn: The cat is lying on the bed.
note: Also "to be located": Var ligger stationen? Irregular: låg, legat.

exEn: We're going to Gothenburg on Friday.
note: By car, bus, train or bike; on foot, use gå. Åka buss = go by bus.

exEn: Can you drive me to the station?
note: k before ö is soft: tj-sound. The driver kör; passengers åker.

exEn: The kids are playing in the park.
note: For children's play. Games, sports and music use spela.

exEn: We play soccer on Saturdays.
note: For games, sports and instruments: spela gitarr. Children's play is leka.

exEn: I usually bike to work.
note: Almost always brukar + verb = usually. Brukade = used to.

en: to have time; to make it
exEn: I don't have time to eat breakfast.
note: Irregular: hann, hunnit. Hinner vi? = Will we make it?

exEn: I don't have the energy to cook tonight.
note: A very Swedish word: to have the energy, or can be bothered (Jag orkar inte!).

ex: Jag bor i en liten {stad} i norra Sverige.
exEn: I live in a small town in northern Sweden.
note: Plural städer. In speech the d is often silent, and staden becomes stan.

ex: Ska vi gå {på stan} på lördag?
exEn: Shall we go into town on Saturday?
note: Stan is everyday Swedish for staden. Gå på stan = go into town to shop or stroll.

ex: Min mormor bor i en liten {by} på landet.
exEn: My grandmother lives in a small village in the country.
note: False friend: by means village. English 'by' is usually av or vid.

exEn: Stockholm is the capital of Sweden.
Are you taking the bus downtown?
note: Usually without an article: i centrum = downtown. Definite: centret or centrumet.

ex: De bor i en {förort} söder om Stockholm.
exEn: They live in a suburb south of Stockholm.
We live in a quiet area.
The bank is two blocks from here.
note: Also the neighborhood around you: i mitt kvarter = in my neighborhood.

exEn: Which street do you live on?
note: You live på a street. In street names it is -gatan: Storgatan.

ex: Kan du visa mig {vägen} till stationen?
exEn: Can you show me the way to the station?
note: Both a road and the way somewhere: fråga om vägen = ask for directions.

exEn: See you in the square at three.
note: Final -rg is pronounced -rj.

ex: Ska vi ta en promenad i {parken}?
exEn: Shall we take a walk in the park?
The children are playing at the playground.
We cycle over the bridge every morning.
There's a café on the corner.
note: Runt hörnet = around the corner.

exEn: There was an accident at the intersection.
Stop! The traffic light is red.
Cross the street at the crosswalk.
note: Drivers must stop for pedestrians at an övergångsställe.

exEn: You're not allowed to cycle on the sidewalk.
Go straight ahead at the roundabout.

ex: Det finns en stor {parkering} bakom affären.
exEn: There's a big parking lot behind the store.
Follow the signs to the town center.
note: sk before y is the sj-sound.

exEn: The city hall is a beautiful building.

ex: Jag går till {affären} och köper mjölk.
exEn: I'm going to the store to buy milk.
note: Also means a business deal or a (love) affair.

exEn: The shop closes at six.
note: A bit more formal than affär; common in compounds: klädbutik = clothing store.

ex: Finns det en {mataffär} här i närheten?
exEn: Is there a grocery store near here?
note: In everyday speech often just affären.

ex: Vi åkte till ett stort {köpcentrum} utanför stan.
exEn: We went to a big shopping mall outside town.
note: The definite form is köpcentret or köpcentrumet.

exEn: The bank opens at ten.
note: Many Swedish bank branches no longer handle cash.

exEn: You can buy painkillers at the pharmacy.
My sister works at the hospital.
note: Be in the hospital = ligga på sjukhus.

ex: Jag har en tid på {vårdcentralen} imorgon.
exEn: I have an appointment at the health center tomorrow.
note: Where you see a doctor for everyday problems; in an emergency you go to akuten.

ex: Vi gifte oss i den här {kyrkan}.
exEn: We got married in this church.
note: k before y is soft: tj-sound.

exEn: The museum is free for children.
note: Irregular: the -um drops in museet, museer.

exEn: I borrow books from the library.
note: False friend: a bookstore is en bokhandel.

ex: Vi äter middag på en italiensk {restaurang}.
exEn: We're having dinner at an Italian restaurant.
note: Spelling trap: it ends in -ang, not -ant.

exEn: We'll meet at the café by the square.
note: Also spelled café.

exEn: Which hotel are you staying at?
note: Stay at a hotel = bo på hotell.

ex: Ska vi gå på {bio} i kväll?
exEn: Shall we go to the movies tonight?
note: Short for biograf. Gå på bio = go to the movies (no article).

exEn: She often goes to the theater.
note: The e drops in the plural: teatrar.

exEn: I'll pick you up at the station.
note: -tion is pronounced with the sj-sound: sta-SHOON.

exEn: I'm getting off at the next stop.

ex: Vi måste vara på {flygplatsen} klockan sju.
exEn: We have to be at the airport at seven.

ex: Jag hittade en plånbok och gick till {polisstationen}.
exEn: I found a wallet and went to the police station.
note: Swedes often just say polisen: Jag gick till polisen.

exEn: She isn't in the office today.

ex: Min pappa jobbade på en {fabrik} i trettio år.
exEn: My dad worked at a factory for thirty years.
The ferry leaves from the harbor at nine.
Take the first street on the right.
note: Till höger = to/on the right. The right one = den högra.

exEn: Turn left at the church.
note: Till vänster = to/on the left. The left one = den vänstra.

ex: Gå {rakt fram} i ungefär hundra meter.
exEn: Go straight ahead for about a hundred meters.
You need to turn right after the bridge.
note: For turning around, use vända.

exEn: The pharmacy is opposite the station.
note: Also written mitt emot.

exEn: The store is quite close.
note: Also a preposition: nära stationen = near the station. Närmare, närmast = closer, closest.

exEn: Is it far to the airport?
note: Långt borta = far away. Opposite: nära.

exEn: Excuse me, where's the nearest restroom?
note: Buildings and places ligger (lie) somewhere: Var ligger banken? = Where is the bank?

exEn: How do I get to the hospital from here?

ex: Vi bor i ett {stort} hus på landet.
exEn: We live in a big house in the countryside.

ex: Vi har en {liten} lägenhet i stan.
exEn: We have a small apartment in town.
note: Irregular: ett litet hus, två små hus. 'The little …' is lilla: den lilla katten.

exEn: My brother is very tall.
note: About people, lång means tall. Comparison with umlaut: längre, längst.

exEn: I have short hair now.
note: Also a noun: ett kort (a card).

exEn: The rent is too high.
note: Also used for volume: hög musik (loud music). Högt is pronounced 'hökt'.

exEn: Prices are low right now.
The bed is 160 centimeters wide.
note: Neuter: brett (ett brett leende, a wide smile).

exEn: The street is too narrow for the bus.
note: A thin person is smal; tunn is for things like paper or ice.

ex: Ta på dig en {tjock} tröja, det är kallt ute.
exEn: Put on a thick sweater, it's cold outside.
note: tj is the soft tj-sound. About people, tjock (fat) can sound rude.

ex: Isen är för {tunn}, gå inte ut på den!
exEn: The ice is too thin, don't walk on it!
note: Neuter: tunt (only one n).

exEn: Have you bought a new bike?
note: Neuter: nytt (double t): ett nytt jobb.

exEn: Our car is pretty old.
note: Irregular: gamla, äldre, äldst. Hur gammal är du? = How old are you?

ex: Hon är för {ung} för att köra bil.
exEn: She is too young to drive.
note: Comparison with umlaut: yngre, yngst.

exEn: That was a really good movie.
note: Bra never changes form (ett bra jobb, bra filmer), but compares irregularly: bättre, bäst.

exEn: The weather is bad today.
note: In everyday speech the g in -ig is usually silent: 'dåli'. Jag mår dåligt = I feel sick.

exEn: It's so warm outside!
note: Also the normal word for hot food and weather: varm mat.

ex: Vattnet är för {kallt} för att bada.
exEn: The water is too cold to swim in.
Careful, the coffee is hot!
note: Stronger than varm: really hot. Neuter: hett.

exEn: The train is faster than the bus.
note: For 'fast' as an adverb, Swedes often say fort: Hon springer fort.

exEn: The computer is so slow today.
note: Double m when an ending is added: långsamma. 'Slowly' is långsamt or sakta.

ex: Det är {dyrt} att bo i Stockholm.
exEn: It's expensive to live in Stockholm.
I found a cheap plane ticket.
Is Swedish easy to learn?
note: Means both easy and light: en lätt väska (a light bag).

exEn: The test was really hard.
Wow, the bag is heavy!
note: Comparison with umlaut: tyngre, tyngst.

exEn: The recipe is simple and tasty.
note: The e drops before an ending: enkla, enklare.

exEn: Is the towel clean?
note: Neuter: rent (one n). Also 'pure': rent vatten.

exEn: Take off your dirty shoes!
The bus was completely full.
note: Colloquially, full also means drunk.

exEn: The fridge is empty, we need to go shopping.
note: Double m when an ending starts with a vowel: tomma.

exEn: Is the store open on Sunday?
note: The e drops in the plural: öppna (same spelling as the verb 'to open').

exEn: The library is closed on Mondays.
note: From stänga (to close). Shop signs say Öppet / Stängt.

exEn: The apartment is big and bright.
note: lj is pronounced j. Also a noun: ett ljus (a light, a candle).

exEn: In winter it gets dark early.
What a soft sweater!
The bed at the hotel was too hard.
note: Hårt is also the adverb: jobba hårt (work hard). 'Difficult' is svår.

exEn: The grass is still wet.
note: Neuter: vått. In everyday speech blöt (soaking wet) is just as common.

exEn: Is the laundry dry yet?
The coffee is too strong for me.
note: Also used for spicy food: stark mat.

exEn: I feel weak after the cold.

ex: Om jag blir {rik} köper jag ett hus vid havet.
exEn: If I get rich, I'll buy a house by the sea.
They were poor but happy.
note: Only 'without money'. For 'poor thing!', say stackars: Stackars dig!

ex: Är det här {rätt} buss till centrum?
exEn: Is this the right bus to the center?
note: Du har rätt = You're right. As an adverb, rätt also means 'quite': rätt bra.

exEn: Sorry, I've dialed the wrong number.
note: Never changes form. As a noun, ett fel is a mistake or fault: Det är mitt fel.

ex: Det är {viktigt} att dricka mycket vatten.
exEn: It's important to drink lots of water.
Are you completely sure about that?
note: Also 'safe': ett säkert ställe. The adverb säkert often means 'probably'.

ex: Det är {farligt} att cykla utan hjälm.
exEn: It's dangerous to cycle without a helmet.
Be quiet, the baby is sleeping!
The neighbors are very loud on weekends.
note: Neuter: högljutt. Loud music is hög musik: Musiken är för hög!

exEn: Stockholm is a beautiful city.
note: The e drops before an ending: vackra, vackrare.

ex: Jag tycker att den lampan är {ful}.
exEn: I think that lamp is ugly.
What nice weather today!
note: A very common compliment: Vad fint! (How nice!)

ex: {Snygg} jacka! Var har du köpt den?
exEn: Nice jacket! Where did you buy it?
note: Snyggt! on its own means 'Nice one!' or 'Well done!'

exEn: What a cute dog!
note: Means both sweet (taste) and cute. Neuter: sött.

exEn: Ugh, the milk has gone sour!
note: About a person it means grumpy: Varför är du sur?

exEn: It was a fun party.
note: Means both fun and funny. Ha det roligt! = Have fun!

exEn: This book is so boring.
note: Det var tråkigt att höra = I'm sorry to hear that.

exEn: It was great to see you!
note: Very common in speech. Never changes form: ett kul jobb, kul filmer.

ex: Är det {möjligt} att betala med kort?
exEn: Is it possible to pay by card?
note: så snart som möjligt = as soon as possible.

ex: Det är {omöjligt} att hitta parkering här.
exEn: It's impossible to find parking here.
note: The prefix o- means 'not' and is said 'oo': olycklig, ovanlig.

ex: Är det {sant} att du ska flytta?
exEn: Is it true that you're moving?
note: Neuter: sant (one n). Sant eller falskt? = True or false?

exEn: We were home all day.
note: Also 'not broken': Koppen är hel. Helt = completely.

exEn: My phone is broken.
note: For things and clothes. A broken bone is bruten.

exEn: Thanks for a lovely evening!
note: Trevlig helg! = Have a nice weekend!

exEn: It's been a tough week.
note: Very common in speech for anything tiring, demanding or annoying.

exEn: What animals are there in Sweden?
note: The d is silent: dj sounds like j. Same form in the plural: ett djur, två djur.

exEn: Do you have any pets?
note: Literally 'house animal'.

exEn: The dog wants to go out.
Our cat sleeps almost all day.
My daughter loves horses.
The farmer has thirty cows.
note: Short forms: kon (the cow), kor (cows), korna (the cows).

exEn: The pig is lying in the mud.
There are lots of sheep on Gotland.
note: Same form in the plural. Don't mix it up with får 'get(s)', from the verb få.

exEn: The goat eats everything it finds.
note: g before e sounds like j. Irregular plural: getter.

exEn: We have five hens in the garden.
note: Chickens as a group are höns (ett): Vi har höns.

exEn: The rooster wakes us up every morning.
The kids want a rabbit.
The cat caught a mouse.
note: Irregular plural: möss, mössen. Also a computer mouse.

exEn: I saw a rat in the subway!
The birds sing early in the morning.
note: The e drops out in the other forms: fågeln, fåglar.

exEn: Drive carefully, there are moose here.
note: Final -lg is pronounced -lj. Called elk in British English.

exEn: There are bears in northern Sweden.
note: Also a common first name: Björn.

exEn: Have you ever seen a wolf?
note: Final -rg is pronounced -rj.

exEn: A fox ran across the road.
A squirrel is climbing up the tree.
The hedgehog comes out in the evening.

ex: En {hare} är större än en kanin.
exEn: A hare is bigger than a rabbit.

ex: Ett {rådjur} har ätit upp våra tulpaner!
exEn: A deer has eaten our tulips!
note: The roe deer, Sweden's most common deer. Same form in the plural.

ex: Vi såg {renar} när vi var i Kiruna.
exEn: We saw reindeer when we were in Kiruna.
note: Same spelling as the adjective ren (clean).

ex: {Sälen} ligger och solar på en sten.
exEn: The seal is lying in the sun on a rock.

ex: Har du sett en {val} på riktigt?
exEn: Have you ever seen a real whale?
note: Ett val is a different word: a choice or an election.

exEn: I'm afraid of snakes.
A frog jumped into the water.
note: At Midsummer, Swedes dance around the maypole to Små grodorna (Little Frogs).

exEn: Spiders aren't insects.

ex: Det sitter en stor {spindel} i badkaret!
exEn: There's a big spider in the bathtub!
note: The e drops out in the other forms: spindeln, spindlar.

exEn: Close the door, or the flies will get in.
I got bitten by a mosquito.
note: As a mass noun, Swedes say mygg: Det är mycket mygg i kväll.

exEn: Bees make honey.
note: A bumblebee is en humla.

ex: Akta dig, det sitter en {geting} på din glass!
exEn: Watch out, there's a wasp on your ice cream!
note: g before e sounds like j: YE-ting.

exEn: A butterfly landed on my hand.
We have ants in the kitchen!
A gull stole my sandwich!
note: The big gulls are also called trut.

exEn: The crow is sitting on the roof.
Owls hunt at night.
The kids are feeding the ducks in the park.
note: Kalle Anka is Donald Duck, whose TV show is a Christmas Eve tradition.

exEn: What beautiful swans!
The lion is the king of the animals.
note: An ett-word, same form in the plural: ett lejon, två lejon.

exEn: The tiger has striped fur.
note: The e drops out in the plural: tigrar.

exEn: Elephants have good memories.
The monkeys at the zoo were so funny!
The giraffe has a very long neck.
note: The g sounds like the sj-sound: shi-RAFF.

exEn: The dog is wagging its tail.
The cat has such soft fur.
note: Also a fur coat.

exEn: The bird has an injured wing.
The cat has hurt its paw.
note: Ge tass! is what you say to a dog for 'Shake!'.

exEn: Don't be scared, the dog doesn't bite.
note: Irregular: bet, bitit. Jag blev biten = I got bitten.

exEn: The neighbor's dog barks all night.
note: sk before ä is the sj-sound. Skälla på någon = to scold someone.

exEn: The cat meows when it's hungry.
note: Also mjaua. A Swedish cat says mjau.

ex: Kan du {mata} katten medan jag är borta?
exEn: Can you feed the cat while I'm away?
note: Easy to remember: mat means food.

exEn: What nice weather we have today!
note: The e drops in the definite form: vädret. Same form in the plural.

exEn: The sun finally came out!
There will be rain this afternoon.
note: gn is pronounced ngn: "rengn".

exEn: The kids are playing in the snow.

ex: Det finns inte ett {moln} på himlen.
exEn: There isn't a cloud in the sky.
note: Same form in the plural: ett moln, många moln.

exEn: There was thick fog this morning.
The dog is scared of thunder.
note: Also a verb: det åskar (it is thundering).

exEn: Lightning struck a tree.
note: Also a camera flash.

exEn: There's supposed to be a storm this weekend.
Don't go out on the ice!
note: False friend: ice cream is glass, not is. Ice cubes are isbitar.

exEn: We got hail in the middle of June!
note: The e drops in the definite form: haglet. It is hailing = det haglar.

exEn: The temperature is dropping tonight.
note: Stress on the last syllable: tempera-TUR.

exEn: It's twenty degrees today.
note: Fem grader varmt = 5 °C above zero, fem grader kallt = 5 °C below zero.

exEn: It was twenty below zero this morning.
note: Mostly used in the plural. The opposite is plusgrader.

exEn: Have you seen the weather forecast for the weekend?
note: Often shortened to prognosen: Vad säger prognosen?

exEn: Don't forget your umbrella, it's going to rain.
note: Stress on the last syllable: para-PLY.

exEn: It's cloudy but quite warm.
note: After det är, weather adjectives take the t-form: det är molnigt, soligt, blåsigt.

exEn: Today it's overcast and gray.
note: The e drops in the plural: mulna. Det är mulet = the sky is completely gray.

exEn: We're hoping for a sunny weekend.
It's very windy by the sea.
It's been a rainy summer.

ex: Ta med en jacka, kvällarna är {kyliga}.
exEn: Bring a jacket, the evenings are chilly.
note: k before y is soft: the tj-sound.

exEn: It's hot and humid today.

ex: Kör försiktigt, det är {halt} på vägarna.
exEn: Drive carefully, the roads are slippery.
note: Det är halt = it is slippery, usually because of ice. The noun is halka.

exEn: It's been raining all day.
note: Weather verbs take det as the subject: det regnar (it is raining).

exEn: Look, it's snowing!
It's really windy today.
note: Det blåser = it's windy (literally 'it blows').

exEn: The sun is shining and it's warm.
note: Irregular: skiner – sken – skinit. sk before i is the sj-sound.

exEn: I'm cold, can we go inside?
note: Jag fryser = I am cold (not jag är kall). Irregular: frös – frusit.

exEn: The snow has started to melt.

ex: {Vad är det för väder} där hos er?
exEn: What's the weather like where you are?
note: Vad är det för …? = what kind of … is it? You can also ask: Hur är vädret?

ex: Vi älskar att vara ute i {naturen}.
exEn: We love being out in nature.
note: Stress on the last syllable: na-TUR.

exEn: The sky is completely blue today.
note: The e drops in the definite form: himlen. Also means heaven.

exEn: I need some fresh air.
We're going for a walk in the woods.
In the summer we swim in the lake.
note: False friend: sjö is a lake, not the sea. The sea is havet.

exEn: We live near the sea.
We climbed up the mountain.
note: rg at the end sounds like rj. Same form in the plural: två berg.

exEn: The kids are sledding on the hill.
note: Uppför backen = uphill, nerför backen = downhill.

exEn: The Nile is the longest river in the world.
note: Rivers in Sweden are usually called älv (large) or å (small).

exEn: A small stream runs through the village.
note: A whole noun in one letter. Many town names end in it: Umeå, Piteå.

exEn: Gotland is Sweden's largest island.
We go sailing in the archipelago every summer.
note: Literally 'skerry garden': the thousands of small islands along the coast.

ex: Ska vi gå till {stranden} i eftermiddag?
exEn: Shall we go to the beach this afternoon?
note: Irregular plural with umlaut: stränder.

exEn: We're renting a cabin on the coast.

ex: Det står ett stort {träd} i trädgården.
exEn: There's a big tree in the garden.
note: Same form in the plural: ett träd, två träd.

exEn: I bought flowers for my mom.

ex: Vi satt i {gräset} och åt glass.
exEn: We sat on the grass eating ice cream.
note: A lawn is a gräsmatta.

exEn: The kids are throwing stones into the water.
I've got sand in my shoes.
I have dirt under my nails.
note: Jorden also means the Earth, the planet.

ex: På hösten blir {löven} gula och röda.
exEn: In the fall the leaves turn yellow and red.
note: Same form in the plural: ett löv, många löv.

exEn: A bird is sitting on a branch.

ex: Titta, man kan se {stjärnorna} i kväll!
exEn: Look, you can see the stars tonight!
note: stj is the sj-sound.

ex: Titta på {månen}, den är så stor!
exEn: Look at the moon, it's so big!

ex: Vi gick upp tidigt för att se {soluppgången}.
exEn: We got up early to see the sunrise.
What a beautiful sunset!
note: sol + ned + gång: literally 'sun-down-going'. The opposite is soluppgång.

exEn: Look, a rainbow over the lake!
Which season do you like best?
note: The four seasons: vår, sommar, höst, vinter.

exEn: The kids bike to school every morning.
note: gå i skolan = to go to (attend) school; i skolan = at school.

ex: Jag hämtar barnen på {förskolan} klockan fyra.
exEn: I pick up the kids from preschool at four.
note: For children aged 1–5. Many people still call it dagis.

ex: Efter {grundskolan} börjar de flesta på gymnasiet.
exEn: After compulsory school, most people start upper secondary school.
note: Years 1–9 (about ages 7–16), free and compulsory for all children.

ex: Min bror går sista året på {gymnasiet}.
exEn: My brother is in his last year of high school.
note: False friend: not a gym (that's ett gym). Usually definite: gå på gymnasiet.

ex: Min syster pluggar på {universitetet} i Göteborg.
exEn: My sister studies at the university in Gothenburg.
note: Stressed on the last syllable: u-ni-ver-si-TET. Same form in the plural.

ex: Jag vill söka till {högskolan} nästa år.
exEn: I want to apply to college next year.
note: Not a high school! It's higher education, like a universitet but usually smaller.

ex: Jag går på {sfi} tre dagar i veckan.
exEn: I go to SFI three days a week.
note: Svenska för invandrare: free Swedish classes for adults new to Sweden. Said as letters (ess-eff-i), used without an article. Also written SFI.

exEn: There are twenty-five students in our class.
note: School years are named by number: Hon går i trean = she's in third grade.

ex: Det är alldeles för varmt i {klassrummet}.
exEn: It's way too warm in the classroom.
note: The m doubles before an ending: klassrummet, klassrummen.

exEn: The school has about five hundred pupils.
note: A pupil at school (also at sfi); at a university you are a student.

exEn: Many students work part-time on weekends.
note: ta studenten = to graduate from upper secondary school, a big celebration with white caps.

exEn: The principal wants to talk to your parents.
note: Also the head of a university. The stress moves in the plural: rektorer is stressed on -tor-.

exEn: The lesson starts at a quarter past eight.
note: -tion is pronounced 'shoon' with the sj-sound.

exEn: Which subject do you like best?
note: Also a topic: byta ämne = to change the subject.

exEn: Have you done your math homework?
note: Countable in Swedish: en läxa (one assignment), många läxor.

exEn: We have an English test tomorrow.
note: skriva prov = to take a test. Same form in the plural.

exEn: She got the highest grade in Swedish.
note: School grades go from A (best) to E (lowest pass); F is a fail.

ex: Jag går en {kurs} i spanska på kvällarna.
exEn: I'm taking a Spanish course in the evenings.
note: gå en kurs = to take a course. The u is short.

exEn: The program takes three years.
note: Education in general, or one study program: en treårig utbildning (a three-year program).

exEn: He graduated in June.
note: Not an exam: ta examen = to graduate. Irregular: the definite form is also examen, the plural examina.

ex: På {rasten} spelar vi fotboll på skolgården.
exEn: At recess we play soccer in the schoolyard.
note: Also a break at work: lunchrast = lunch break.

ex: Har du sett {schemat} för nästa vecka?
exEn: Have you seen the schedule for next week?
note: sch is the sj-sound, as in schampo.

exEn: The new semester starts in August.
note: False friend: semester means vacation in Swedish! hösttermin = fall semester, vårtermin = spring semester.

exEn: The kids are off school all next week.
note: School breaks: sommarlov, jullov, sportlov. Working adults have semester instead.

ex: Jag har lånat en {bok} på biblioteket.
exEn: I've borrowed a book from the library.
note: Irregular plural: en bok, två böcker.

exEn: Open your books to page twenty.
note: Also a side: på andra sidan gatan = across the street.

exEn: Can I borrow a pen?
note: Any pen or pencil. To be exact: blyertspenna (pencil), kulspetspenna (ballpoint pen).

exEn: Write your name at the top of the paper.
note: Also documents: Har du dina papper? (Do you have your papers?)

exEn: Cut out the picture with a pair of scissors.
note: Singular in Swedish: en sax = a pair of scissors.

exEn: The teacher writes the words on the board.
note: Also a painting or picture on the wall.

exEn: Look the word up in a dictionary.
note: slå upp = to look up. Plural like bok: ordböcker.

exEn: How long have you been studying Swedish?
note: Languages are lowercase in Swedish. en svenska also means a Swedish woman.

exEn: We have English every Tuesday.
note: Many language names end in -ska: engelska, svenska, tyska, franska, spanska.

exEn: Math is my favorite subject.
note: Short for matematik.

exEn: He's very interested in history.
note: Also a story: Berätta en historia! (Tell me a story!)

exEn: How many languages do you speak?
note: Same form in the plural: ett språk, två språk.

exEn: What does this word mean?
note: Same form in the plural: ett ord, två ord.

exEn: Write a sentence with each word.
note: Also meaning or purpose: Vad är meningen med det? (What's the point of that?)

exEn: Your pronunciation is getting better and better!
note: From uttala (to pronounce): Hur uttalar man det här?

exEn: May I ask a question?
note: ställa en fråga = to ask a question. Also a verb: fråga (to ask).

exEn: Do you know the answer to question three?
note: svaret på = the answer to. The verb is svara (to answer).

exEn: Do exercise five for next time.
note: Övning ger färdighet = practice makes perfect.

ex: Alla gör {misstag} när de lär sig ett språk.
exEn: Everyone makes mistakes when they learn a language.
note: göra ett misstag = to make a mistake. In speech, people also say göra fel.

ex: Alla i klassen blev {godkända} på provet.
exEn: Everyone in the class passed the test.
note: bli godkänd = to pass; the opposite is underkänd (failed). Many courses grade G (pass), VG (pass with distinction) or U (fail).

ex: Jag måste {plugga} inför provet på fredag.
exEn: I have to study for the test on Friday.
note: The everyday word for studying; studera sounds more formal.

exEn: She's studying law in Uppsala.
note: In speech Swedes often say läsa: Jag läser svenska = I'm studying Swedish.

ex: Barn {lär sig} nya språk väldigt snabbt.
exEn: Children learn new languages very quickly.
note: sig changes with the person: jag lär mig, du lär dig, vi lär oss.

exEn: Dad taught me to ride a bike.
note: lära någon något = to teach someone something. With sig it means to learn.

exEn: I practice my pronunciation every day.
note: öva på något = to practice something.

exEn: How do you spell your last name?
note: Hur stavas det? = How is that spelled?

ex: Jag är {sjuk} och stannar hemma idag.
exEn: I'm sick and staying home today.
note: Bli sjuk = to get sick. Sj is the breathy sj-sound.

exEn: Now I'm well again!
note: Not 'frisky'. Bli frisk = to get well. It also means 'fresh': frisk luft (fresh air).

exEn: Smoking is bad for your health.
note: Don't mix it up with the verb hälsa (to greet).

exEn: Diabetes is a common disease.
I'm not feeling very well today.
note: Hur mår du? = How are you? Må bra / må dåligt = to feel good / to feel bad.

ex: Jag {mår illa} och vill inte äta.
exEn: I feel nauseous and don't want to eat.
note: It means nausea, not just feeling bad: for that, say må dåligt.

exEn: I'm so tired today.
note: Trött på = tired of: Jag är trött på regnet.

ex: Jag blir {yr} när jag reser mig.
exEn: I get dizzy when I stand up.
My head hurts.
note: Ha ont i + body part in the definite form: ont i magen, ont i halsen.

exEn: It hurts when I walk.
note: Aj, det gör ont! = Ouch, that hurts!

exEn: My back is aching.
note: A dull, lasting pain. Common in compounds: huvudvärk, tandvärk.

exEn: How bad is the pain right now?
note: More formal than ont; used by doctors and on medicine packages.

ex: Jag har {huvudvärk} och vill vila lite.
exEn: I have a headache and want to rest a bit.
note: No article: Jag har huvudvärk. Also: Jag har ont i huvudet.

exEn: The kids got a stomachache from all the ice cream.
note: Also: ont i magen.

ex: Drick te med honung om du har {halsont}.
exEn: Drink tea with honey if you have a sore throat.
note: Also: ont i halsen.

ex: Jag har {tandvärk} och måste till tandläkaren.
exEn: I have a toothache and have to go to the dentist.

ex: Han har haft hög {feber} sedan igår.
exEn: He has had a high fever since yesterday.
note: No article: Jag har feber (I have a fever).

exEn: I have a bit of a cold today.
note: Swedes usually say Jag är förkyld rather than Jag har en förkylning.

exEn: It's just a common cold.
note: k before y is soft (the tj-sound): för-TJYL-ning.

ex: Många är sjuka i {influensa} just nu.
exEn: Lots of people have the flu right now.
note: Sjuk i influensa = sick with the flu. Colloquially also flunsa.

ex: Jag har haft {hosta} i två veckor.
exEn: I've had a cough for two weeks.
note: No article: Jag har hosta (I have a cough).

exEn: He coughed all night.

ex: Jag har {snuva} och ont i halsen.
exEn: I have a runny nose and a sore throat.
note: A stuffy nose is täppt näsa: Jag är täppt i näsan.

exEn: I'm sneezing all the time.
note: Past also nyste. When someone sneezes, say Prosit! (Bless you!)

exEn: She's been throwing up all night.
note: An -s verb in every form: kräks, kräktes, kräkts. In everyday speech also spy.

exEn: Do you have any allergies?
note: Stress on the last syllable, and the g is hard. Allergisk mot = allergic to.

ex: Är det {smittsamt}? Kan jag gå till jobbet?
exEn: Is it contagious? Can I go to work?
note: From smitta: infection (noun) or to infect (verb).

exEn: My arm itches.
note: Usually with det: Det kliar (It itches).

exEn: It's not a serious injury.
note: Also a verb: skada (to injure, to damage).

exEn: She fell and hurt herself.
note: Reflexive: jag skadar mig, du skadar dig, hon skadar sig.

exEn: Wash the wound with soap and water.
Your nose is bleeding!

ex: Jag fick ett stort {blåmärke} på benet.
exEn: I got a big bruise on my leg.
note: Literally 'blue mark'.

exEn: He has broken his arm.
note: Irregular: bröt, brutit. Use the definite form for your own body: bryta benet. Broken = bruten (benet är brutet).

exEn: She fainted in the heat.
The ambulance came after ten minutes.
note: The ending is usually said -angs, as in many French loanwords.

exEn: Quick, call an ambulance!
note: The emergency number in Sweden is 112 (ett ett två).

ex: Vi åkte till {akuten} mitt i natten.
exEn: We went to the ER in the middle of the night.
note: Almost always used in the definite form: akuten. As an adjective, akut means 'acute, urgent'.

exEn: You should go to the doctor.
note: The official word is läkare; doktor is common in speech and as a title.

en: I need to see a doctor
exEn: I need to see a doctor today.
note: Träffa (to meet) is also used for seeing a doctor.

exEn: The patient can go home today.
note: The ti is said like 'si': pa-si-ENT.

ex: Jag har en {tid} hos läkaren klockan tre.
exEn: I have a doctor's appointment at three.
note: Usually 'time'; in healthcare, en tid is an appointment.

exEn: I called the health center and made an appointment.
note: You can often book online through 1177.se.

en: to call the health advice line
ex: Om du blir sämre kan du {ringa 1177}.
exEn: If you get worse, you can call 1177.
note: 1177 (elva sjuttiosju) is Sweden's healthcare advice line, open 24/7. In an emergency, call 112.

exEn: The doctor examined my knee.
note: En undersökning = an examination, a check-up.

ex: – {Var gör det ont}? – Här, i knät.
exEn: – Where does it hurt? – Here, in my knee.
Breathe calmly and deeply.
note: An -s verb in every form: andas, andades, andats. Andas in / ut = breathe in / out.

ex: Läkaren skrev ut ett {recept} på antibiotika.
exEn: The doctor wrote a prescription for antibiotics.
note: Also means 'recipe'. Receptfri medicin = over-the-counter medicine.

exEn: Have you taken your medicine today?
note: c before i is said like s. Ta medicin = to take medicine.

ex: Ta en {tablett} tre gånger om dagen.
exEn: Take one pill three times a day.

ex: Ta en {värktablett} och lägg dig och vila.
exEn: Take a painkiller and lie down and rest.
note: Many Swedes just say the brand names Alvedon or Ipren.

ex: Har du ett {plåster}? Jag har skurit mig.
exEn: Do you have a Band-Aid? I've cut myself.
note: The e drops out in plåstret and plåstren.

exEn: I've been vaccinated against the flu.
note: cc is said ks: vak-SIN. Vaccinera sig = to get vaccinated.

exEn: You need to rest for a few days.

ex: Det finns inget som kan {bota} en förkylning.
exEn: There's nothing that can cure a cold.
Did you forget to turn off the stove?
note: En öppen spis is a fireplace.

exEn: Set the oven to 200 degrees.
note: g before n sounds like ng: "ungn".

ex: Kör den i {mikron} i två minuter.
exEn: Put it in the microwave for two minutes.
note: Everyday short form of mikrovågsugn.

exEn: The milk is in the fridge.
note: Often just kylen: Lägg det i kylen. k before y is soft (tj-sound).

exEn: There's ice cream in the freezer.
note: Related verb: frysa (to freeze). Jag fryser = I'm cold.

exEn: Can you empty the dishwasher?
Put the dirty dishes in the sink.
note: Also called diskho. A bathroom sink is a handfat.

exEn: We've bought a new coffee maker.
note: Like most -are words, the plural is the same: två kaffebryggare.

exEn: Should I put the kettle on?
note: Literally "water boiler".

exEn: I'm making toast in the toaster.
note: Toast is rostat bröd (toasted bread).

exEn: Boil water in a large saucepan.
note: Stress on the second syllable: kas-TRULL.

ex: Hetta upp lite olja i en {stekpanna}.
exEn: Heat a little oil in a frying pan.
note: Often just pannan in everyday speech.

ex: Lägg på ett {lock}, så kokar vattnet snabbare.
exEn: Put a lid on, and the water will boil faster.
note: False friend: a lock (for a door) is ett lås.

exEn: This knife is really sharp.
note: Unlike in English, the k is pronounced: k-niv.

exEn: Can I have a clean fork?
note: The plural drops the e: gafflar.

exEn: You eat soup with a spoon.
note: sk before e is the sj-sound.

ex: Jag tar en {tesked} socker i teet.
exEn: I take a teaspoon of sugar in my tea.
note: Written tsk in recipes.

exEn: Two tablespoons of sugar is enough.
note: Written msk in recipes.

exEn: The silverware is in the top drawer.
note: Knives, forks and spoons together. Stress on -stick.

ex: Ta en {tallrik} och ta för dig!
exEn: Grab a plate and help yourself!
Can I have a glass of water?
note: Same form in the plural: två glas. Don't mix it up with glass, which means ice cream!

exEn: Would you like a cup of coffee?
note: No word for "of": en kopp te = a cup of tea.

ex: Jag dricker te ur en stor {mugg}.
exEn: I drink tea from a big mug.
note: You drink ur (out of) a cup or mug.

exEn: Get out a big bowl.
note: Skål! on its own means Cheers!

ex: Hämta en {skärbräda} och en vass kniv.
exEn: Get a cutting board and a sharp knife.
note: From skära (to cut) + bräda (board).

exEn: Who does the cooking at your house?
note: Laga on its own usually means to fix: laga cykeln.

exEn: Boil the potatoes for twenty minutes.
note: Also used for coffee: koka kaffe = to make coffee.

exEn: Fry the meatballs in butter.
note: Also used for roasting meat in the oven.

exEn: We baked cinnamon buns over the weekend.
Should we have a barbecue tonight?
He cut the tomatoes into pieces.
note: Irregular: skär, skar, skurit. sk before ä is the sj-sound.

exEn: Chop the onion finely.
Can you peel the potatoes?
note: Ett skal is a peel or shell.

exEn: Keep stirring the sauce.
note: Röra om = to give it a stir. Rör inte! = Don't touch!

ex: {Blanda} mjöl och socker i en skål.
exEn: Mix the flour and sugar in a bowl.
Can you whip the cream?
note: The tool is en visp (a whisk).

exEn: This tastes really good!
note: Vill du smaka? = Would you like a taste?

exEn: I'm heating up some soup for lunch.
Pour the milk into a saucepan.
note: Hälla upp = to pour a drink: Ska jag hälla upp kaffe?

exEn: Whose turn is it to do the dishes?
note: The dirty dishes are disken: Jag tar disken = I'll do the dishes.

ex: Kan du {duka}? Maten är snart klar.
exEn: Can you set the table? The food's almost ready.
note: From en duk (a tablecloth).

ex: Kan du hjälpa mig att {duka av}?
exEn: Can you help me clear the table?
note: The stress is on av.

exEn: What ingredients do we need?
note: Stress on the last syllable: ingredi-ENS.

exEn: What spices have you put in the stew?
note: Also a verb: krydda (kryddar) = to season.

exEn: You need three deciliters of milk.
note: Swedish recipes use dl: 1 dl = 100 ml, a little under half a cup.

exEn: Bring a liter of water to a boil.
note: Same form in the plural: två liter.

exEn: A pack of butter is 500 grams.
note: Same form in the plural: 200 gram.

exEn: The chicken is still raw inside.
note: Ett-form rått: rått kött = raw meat.

exEn: We're having boiled potatoes with the fish.
note: From koka. Kokt potatis is a classic Swedish side dish.

ex: Jag vill ha ett {stekt} ägg, tack.
exEn: I'd like a fried egg, please.
note: From steka.

ex: Det är en härlig {känsla} att vara hemma igen.
exEn: It's a wonderful feeling to be home again.
note: Jag har en känsla av att … = I have a feeling that …

ex: Jag {känner mig} hemma i Sverige nu.
exEn: I feel at home in Sweden now.
note: sig changes with the person: jag känner mig, du känner dig. Känn dig som hemma! = Make yourself at home!

ex: Jag är så {glad} att du kom!
exEn: I'm so happy you came!
note: The everyday word for happy. Neuter: glatt.

exEn: She was sad when the cat died.
note: The d is silent: 'lessen'. Jag är ledsen can also mean I'm sorry.

exEn: Mom gets angry when we fight.
note: -rg is pronounced 'rj'. arg på någon = angry with someone.

exEn: I'm afraid of spiders.
note: rädd för = afraid of. The neuter form rätt is rare.

ex: Och så levde de {lyckliga} i alla sina dagar.
exEn: And they lived happily ever after.
note: Deeper and more lasting than glad. False friend: it doesn't mean lucky (that's ha tur).

ex: Han var {olycklig} på sitt gamla jobb.
exEn: He was unhappy at his old job.
note: The prefix o- often means un-: olycklig, otålig, oärlig.

exEn: Are you happy with the food?
note: nöjd med = happy with. Opposite: missnöjd (dissatisfied).

ex: Min pappa är en väldigt {lugn} person.
exEn: My dad is a very calm person.
note: gn is pronounced 'ngn'. Ta det lugnt! = Take it easy!

ex: Jag är alltid {nervös} innan ett prov.
exEn: I'm always nervous before a test.

ex: Hon är väldigt {stressad} på jobbet just nu.
exEn: She's really stressed at work right now.
note: The verb stressa also means to rush: Stressa inte! = Take your time!

ex: Jag blir {orolig} när du inte svarar.
exEn: I get worried when you don't answer.
note: orolig för = worried about. The noun is oro (worry).

ex: Jag blir {irriterad} när folk kommer för sent.
exEn: I get annoyed when people are late.
note: The verb is irritera: Det irriterar mig = It annoys me.

exEn: I'm a bit disappointed with the result.
note: besviken på = disappointed in/with. Plural: besvikna.

ex: Jag blev {förvånad} när jag såg priset.
exEn: I was surprised when I saw the price.

ex: Barnen är {uttråkade} och vill gå hem.
exEn: The kids are bored and want to go home.
note: Don't mix them up: Jag är uttråkad = I'm bored, but Jag är tråkig = I'm boring!

exEn: I feel lonely sometimes.
note: Means both alone and lonely: Hon bor ensam. Plural doubles the m: ensamma.

ex: Jag tror att jag är {kär} i dig.
exEn: I think I'm in love with you.
note: kär i = in love with; bli kär = to fall in love. Also 'dear': Kära Anna (in letters).

exEn: We're so proud of you!
note: stolt över = proud of.

ex: Jag är väldigt {tacksam} för din hjälp.
exEn: I'm very grateful for your help.
note: tacksam för = grateful for. Plural doubles the m: tacksamma.

ex: Jag är så {avundsjuk} på din semester!
exEn: I'm so jealous of your vacation!
note: avundsjuk på = jealous of. Jealousy in a relationship is svartsjuk.

ex: Jag blev så {generad} när jag ramlade.
exEn: I was so embarrassed when I fell over.
note: From French gêné, so the g is pronounced like sj.

exEn: She's in a bad mood today.
note: False friend: humör means mood (the Swedish for humor is humor). på bra/dåligt humör = in a good/bad mood.

exEn: She cried with joy.
note: The noun of glad. No plural.

exEn: Love is the most important thing in life.
note: The verb is älska. Mostly uncountable, but en stor kärlek = a great love.

ex: Det var en stor {sorg} när mormor dog.
exEn: It was a great sorrow when Grandma died.
note: -rg is pronounced 'rj': sorj.

ex: Hon var röd i ansiktet av {ilska}.
exEn: She was red in the face with anger.
note: The adjective is arg.

ex: Min största {rädsla} är att bli ensam.
exEn: My biggest fear is being alone.
note: rädsla för = fear of. The adjective is rädd.

exEn: We laughed all evening.
note: skratta åt = to laugh at. The noun is ett skratt (a laugh).

exEn: She smiled at me.
note: Irregular: ler, log, lett. le mot = to smile at. The noun is ett leende (a smile).

exEn: The baby cried all night.
note: Irregular: grät, gråtit.

exEn: Don't worry, it'll work out.
note: oroa sig för = to worry about. sig changes with the person: jag oroar mig, du oroar dig.

exEn: I'm ashamed of what I said.
note: Ends in -s in every form: skäms, skämdes, skämts. Skäms på dig! = Shame on you!

exEn: I can't wait for summer!
note: längta efter = to long for; längta till = can't wait for; längta hem = to be homesick.

exEn: I miss you so much!
note: Missing a bus is missa; missing a person or place is sakna.

ex: Vi {trivs} jättebra i vår nya lägenhet.
exEn: We really like it in our new apartment.
note: Ends in -s in every form: trivs, trivdes, trivts. trivas med = to get on well with: Jag trivs med mina kollegor.

exEn: I care about you.
note: Very common in the negative: Jag bryr mig inte = I don't care.

exEn: I hate waiting.
note: The opposite of älska. The noun is ett hat (hatred).

exEn: That's so kind of you!
note: To children it means well-behaved: Var snäll nu!

ex: Var inte så {elak} mot din bror!
exEn: Don't be so mean to your brother!
note: elak mot någon = mean to someone.

ex: Var {ärlig} nu, gillar du min tröja?
exEn: Be honest, do you like my sweater?
note: Ärligt talat = to be honest, honestly.

exEn: He's a bit shy at first.

ex: Han är väldigt {social} och älskar fester.
exEn: He's very sociable and loves parties.
You were so brave at the dentist!

ex: Han är för {feg} för att säga sanningen.
exEn: He's too cowardly to tell the truth.
I've been lazy all weekend.
note: Neuter with double t: latt.

exEn: She's a very hard-working student.
note: The opposite of lat.

exEn: You're so good at Swedish!
note: duktig på = good at. Used about people; for things, say bra.

ex: Hon är {smart} och lär sig snabbt.
exEn: She's smart and learns quickly.

ex: Det var {dumt} av mig att säga så.
exEn: It was stupid of me to say that.
note: Children also use it for mean: Du är dum!

ex: Min dotter är lika {envis} som jag.
exEn: My daughter is as stubborn as I am.

ex: Man måste vara {tålmodig} med små barn.
exEn: You have to be patient with small children.
note: Opposite: otålig (impatient). A patient at the doctor's is en patient.

exEn: Our neighbors are very helpful.
note: hj is pronounced j: the h is silent.

exEn: The milk is in the fridge.
note: Cities and countries take i: i Sverige. With time it can mean 'for': i två år (for two years).

exEn: The book is on the table.
note: Also used for many places and events: på jobbet (at work), på bio (at the movies), på svenska (in Swedish).

exEn: We're going to Gothenburg tomorrow.
note: Also for whom something is meant: en present till dig (a present for you).

exEn: The train from Malmö is delayed.
I drink coffee with milk.
note: The d is often silent: 'me'. With transport it means 'by': med tåg (by train).

ex: Jag vill ha en kaffe {och} en kanelbulle.
exEn: I'd like a coffee and a cinnamon bun.
note: Usually pronounced 'å' in speech.

ex: Det är kallt ute, {men} solen skiner.
